text.p: Lithuanian newspapers carried the following reports in their Friday editions. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy:
- The Klaipeda fishing company Jura, with assets estimated at one billion litas, was closed recently but prosecutors cannot name those guilty of squandering the funds.
- The new government wants to impose stricter legislative measures on those who avoid paying taxes.
- Latvian Prime Minister Andris Shkele arrives in Vilnius on for a one-day unofficial visit to meet Lithuanian counterpart Gediminas Vagnorius and to discuss the bilateral relations.
- The Bank of Lithuania will preserve a fixed and stable litas rate of four to one dollar in the nearest years, the chairman of the bank said.
- Vagnorius said the implementation of the 1996 budget was the worst in Lithuania's history. The year ended with 356 million litas of uncolllected revenues.

- Indictments against the suspected leader of the Kaunas criminal world, Henrikas Daktaras, were based on video and audio recordings made in his car in spring 1995. Businessman Sigitas Ciapas, with whom Daktaras talked, has been shot and the newspaper publishes extracts from the discussion.
- Administration reform aims at two major things -- to decentralise power, the minister of administration reforms and municipalities tells the newspaper.
- Lithuanian lawmakers imposed stricter penalties of up to 10 years of inprisonment against people making toxic alcoholic drinks which may harm other peoples health.

- German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel assured Lithuania that Germany will continue to support Baltic membership of the European Union and NATO during the visit of Lithuanian Foreign Minister Algirdas Saudargas to Berlin.

- Birute Visokaviciene, the head of parliament's social affairs and labour committee, said the abolition of tax privileges to Vilnius, Hermis and Ukio banks provided by the law on foreign capital investments would increase the revenues of the social security and pensions fund. Bankers think that such a move would cause more harm than benefits.

- The U.S. West company, which owns 49 percent of Lithuanian-Dutch telephone exchange company Lintel, decided to sell its shares worth some 28 million litas to Lietuvos Telekomas. The Communications Ministry thinks this permit the reduction of tariffs for international calls.
- The stock exchange plans to form an official trading list in March formed from the four of five most traded and most reliable Lithuanian firms.
